\NLFrontMatterSection{Executive summary}

This architecture baseline supplies the component layer beneath all 1071 sub-interface requirements (SIRs). Each SIR receives a complete logical allocation consisting of a five-component universal interface stack, the components required by its realization package, and the specialized components required by every interface family inherited from its high-level interface requirement (HLIR). The result is a traceable bridge from interface obligation to buildable services, controlled artifacts, accountable teams, tests, commissioning evidence, and release controls.

The components are logical responsibilities rather than mandated products, microservices, vendors, or deployment units. Architecture may combine several responsibilities into one controlled implementation or separate one responsibility across multiple implementations, but it may not delete an obligation, conceal a system boundary, bypass deterministic safety and human approval, or treat transport success as clinical acceptance. Existing commissioned treatment planning systems (TPSs), PACS, oncology information systems, imaging, registration, dose, QA, and delivery systems retain their approved authority. Radiation oncologists, dosimetrists, qualified medical physicists, therapists, informatics personnel, and other authorized professionals retain their specialty decisions and approvals.

\section{1. Purpose, scope, and realization chain}
The controlled trace path addressed by this document is:
\begin{center}
\textbf{ConOps} $\rightarrow$ \textbf{119 HLRs} $\rightarrow$ \textbf{357 HLIRs} $\rightarrow$ \textbf{1071 SIRs} $\rightarrow$ \textbf{61 interface components and 15 teams} $\rightarrow$ \textbf{verified routes and released capability}
\end{center}
The parallel functional branch remains ConOps $\rightarrow$ HLRs $\rightarrow$ 357 detailed sub-requirements $\rightarrow$ 45 functional components. A clinical capability exists only when both branches, their shared hazards and controls, their functional and interface components, their people and procedures, and their verification and commissioning evidence are integrated and accepted together.

This document defines the component responsibilities necessary for implementation planning. It does not prescribe the final topology, technology stack, supplier, site configuration, clinical tolerance, DICOM object inventory, API, or workflow. Those choices remain controlled design and commissioning decisions constrained by the parent requirements.

\section{2. Allocation and interpretation rules}
Each row in Section 9 is complete only when \textbf{I-STACK plus every listed direct component} is implemented and integrated for the actual route. Direct components are derived deterministically from the SIR realization package and every interface family assigned to the parent HLIR. Duplicate components are shown once. Component IDs are stable logical identifiers; implementation identifiers, repositories, services, suppliers, and deployed instances shall trace to them.
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{No component-only closure.} Allocation does not satisfy an SIR. Each component must have an approved specification, implementation or controlled procedure, interface contract, security and resilience controls, verification evidence, anomaly disposition, commissioning evidence where applicable, monitoring, support, and release approval.
\item \textbf{No hidden boundary.} Human-mediated, internal, file, queue, event, DICOM, DICOMweb, IHE, vendor-API, and external-TPS routes receive the same identity, semantics, state, error, audit, reconciliation, and release discipline appropriate to their risk.
\item \textbf{Authority does not move with data.} A successful message, store, import, calculation request, model response, or API call does not create professional approval, physics review, QA completion, transfer authorization, or treatment-delivery authority.
\item \textbf{Family obligations accumulate.} A route assigned to several families must implement the union of their components and subprofiles. Tailoring requires approved trace, risk, clinical, architecture, security, and V\&V rationale.
\item \textbf{Logical allocation permits controlled consolidation.} A deployment may consolidate components when independence, least privilege, failure containment, testability, auditability, supplier responsibility, and rollback remain demonstrable.
\end{itemize}

\section{3. Interface architecture and external TPS boundary}
Every state-changing route shall implement the following controlled chain: authorized producer or user $\rightarrow$ trusted gateway $\rightarrow$ context, schema, semantic, security, and safety validation $\rightarrow$ atomic transaction or bounded human interaction $\rightarrow$ authoritative consumer or system of record $\rightarrow$ explicit layered acknowledgment $\rightarrow$ reconciliation, monitoring, and retained evidence. The chain preserves patient and case identity, professional authority, object and configuration version, lifecycle state, provenance, integrity, failure status, and correlation end to end.

For an external TPS, DICOM and DICOM-RT are the minimum portable exchange foundation. The deployed route shall be bounded by IC-TPS-01 and shall use IC-DCM-01 or IC-DWP-01, IC-RTP-01, IC-DVA-01, IC-CAP-01, IC-ACK-01, and IC-REC-01 as applicable. An optional IC-VAP-01 or IC-IHE-01 route supplements this boundary only when approved and commissioned; it does not bypass authoritative DICOM objects, TPS state, professional approvals, physics review, independent QA, destination verification, or release controls.

The locked planning references for this baseline are \href{https://dicom.nema.org/medical/dicom/current/output/chtml/part02/sect_n.3.3.html}{DICOM PS3.2 2026c Conformance}, \href{https://dicom.nema.org/medical/dicom/current/output/chtml/part04/sect_6.7.html}{DICOM PS3.4 2026c Service Class Specifications}, \href{https://dicom.nema.org/medical/dicom/current/output/chtml/part07/chapter_1.html}{DICOM PS3.7 2026c Message Exchange}, \href{https://dicom.nema.org/medical/dicom/current/output/chtml/part15/PS3.15.html}{DICOM PS3.15 2026c Security and System Management Profiles}, applicable radiotherapy information-object definitions in DICOM PS3.3, and the \href{https://profiles.ihe.net/RO/index.html}{IHE Radiation Oncology Technical Framework, Revision 4.0, 13 May 2026}. DICOM conformance facilitates first-level comparison but does not guarantee interoperability; paired conformance analysis and validation with the actual equipment and workflow are therefore realized by IC-DVA-01, IC-ITL-01, IC-COM-01, and IC-RLS-01.

\section{4. Universal interface realization stack}
Every SIR uses the following universal stack, shown as \textbf{I-STACK} in the allocation tables:
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{IC-BND-01}: one canonical boundary and route identity with accountable ownership.
\item \textbf{IC-CFG-01}: one signed effective interface configuration and compatibility baseline.
\item \textbf{IC-IAM-01}: attributable human and service identity, role, purpose, and approval context.
\item \textbf{IC-AUD-01}: immutable correlated action, decision, version, state, outcome, and exception evidence.
\item \textbf{IC-TRC-01}: bidirectional trace from requirements and hazards through components, tests, results, anomalies, changes, and releases.
\end{itemize}

\section{8. Team-of-teams integration and component definition of done}
The parent SIR owner is accountable for delivery. Package and family leads provide their controlled components. T-SYS integrates the route and safety behavior; T-DATA controls semantics and provenance; T-SEC controls trust and privacy; T-OPS controls transaction and continuity behavior; T-INT controls external clinical interoperability; T-VV remains organizationally independent for required assurance; T-GOV controls activation and change; and the applicable clinical specialties approve the clinical workflow and professional decisions.

A component contribution is complete for an SIR only when:
\begin{itemize}
\item the component specification identifies purpose, authority, inputs, outputs, schema, semantics, preconditions, state, errors, security, timing, dependencies, limitations, normal and degraded behavior, ownership, and support;
\item the implementation or controlled procedure is configuration-managed, reproducible, least-privileged, observable, fail-closed where safety requires, and integrated without an undocumented dependency or unapproved fallback;
\item contract, positive, negative, boundary, wrong-context, stale-version, security, timeout, duplicate, partial, cancellation, recovery, and misuse tests are executed as applicable with retained actual results;
\item actual producers and consumers, TPS vendor and version, site, machine, modality, technique, workflow, and representative clinical cases are commissioned where applicable;
\item failures and anomalies are resolved or formally dispositioned, residual risk is accepted by the proper authority, and monitoring, incident, rollback, revalidation, supplier, and retirement controls are active; and
\item the trace repository demonstrates that no SIR clause, family subprofile, hazard control, professional authority, physics or dosimetry responsibility, independent QA obligation, or release condition was lost during component consolidation or deployment.
\end{itemize}

\section{12. Controlled open interface-component decisions}
The following decisions remain deployment-specific and shall be resolved through controlled architecture, clinical governance, vendor coordination, cybersecurity, operations, verification, commissioning, and change control before an affected route is activated:
\begin{itemize}
\item final component consolidation or separation, implementation technology, hosting, network zones, availability domains, data residency, repositories, queues, events, services, deployment topology, and supplier boundaries;
\item exact producers, consumers, users, systems of record, application entities, endpoints, directions, triggers, interaction modes, workflow states, authority limits, support ownership, and service levels;
\item exact DICOM SOP Classes and roles, transfer syntaxes, DIMSE and DICOMweb services, IHE-RO profiles and options, media profiles, private attributes, vendor APIs, and unsupported, coerced, specialized, extended, or lossy behavior;
\item disease-site, modality, technique, machine, prescription, image, registration, contour, plan, dose, robustness, approval, QA, transfer, and delivery-record semantics requiring site- or vendor-specific profiles;
\item terminology, identifiers, UID creation and preservation, reference graphs, units, coordinates, dose basis, precision, rounding, state mappings, source precedence, acknowledgment layers, and conflict rules;
\item identity federation, role and approval mappings, certificates, secrets, encryption, segmentation, egress, minimum-necessary data, retention, privacy, audit transport, detection, response, and supplier access;
\item performance, capacity, availability, clock tolerance, timeout, retry, ordering, idempotency, cancellation, compensation, quarantine, downtime, recovery, reconciliation, monitoring, and alert thresholds; and
\item final test cases, datasets, tolerances and sources, independence, representative users and cases, vendor and site commissioning, acceptance criteria, anomaly disposition, residual risk, revalidation triggers, rollback, retirement, and release evidence.
\end{itemize}
\textbf{Bottom line. }A sub-interface requirement is brought into being only when its universal, realization-package, and interface-family components operate together across the actual team-of-teams route, preserve clinical professional authority, reconcile with commissioned external TPS and DICOM state, and have objective acceptance and release evidence.
